utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you call the case, please. I think I didn't have my microphone. Would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour, this is case number IT-04-82-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, welcome to all of you. First of all, I would like to ask the accused whether they can hear the proceedings in a language which they understand. Now, Mr. Boskoski, do you understand the proceedings in your language? Is it okay? Do you understand it? Yes. Thank you. But I have no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: His microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Would you please turn on your microphone. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] I do understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tarculovski, how about you? Do you understand our proceedings in your own language? THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask for appearances for the accused. Who is representing the accused Mr. Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour, for the accused Boskoski, Dragan Godzo accompanied by co-attorney Edina Residovic and Jesenka Residovic, the case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And for Mr. Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: Good day, Your Honour. For Mr. Johan Tarculovski, attorney Antonio Apostolski, his Defence attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And who is representing the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, Your Honour, with my colleague, Anees Ahmed, and case manager, Salla Moilanen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The reasons for the Status Conference I think are quite clear to you, but I would like to pronounce it also for the public. The last Status Conference was held on August the 19th of this year. The Trial Chamber is required, pursuant to Rule 65 bis, to hold a Status Conference within 120 days after the initial appearance, or later on, in a similar time, to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure expeditious preparation for trial; secondly, to allow the accused to raise issues in relation to his or her mental and physical condition. Now, as it is provided for by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal in preparation of this Status Conference there was a so-called Rule 65 ter Conference which took place last Friday on the 9th of December which was led by the senior legal officer of Trial Chamber II. I have been fully briefed of the discussions that took place during that conference, and for that reason I think there is no need that we repeat everything what had been discussed in this last conference, but still there are quite a few items which we should address and should talk about. My first point would be the indictment and the pre-trial brief as far as we already got them. In the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, there was at least one point which was also addressed in the order of this Trial Chamber where we had observed a contradiction between paragraph 11 of the amended indictment, which refers to Boskoski's superior responsibility for the acts of prison guards, hospital personnel, and other civilians, in paragraph 83 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. And also, we already had talked about this issue in the 65 ter Conference. I would like to ask the Prosecution whether you would be prepared to provide further information about the position regarding the relationship between pleading command responsibility in paragraph 11 of the amended indictment and command responsibility as described in paragraph 83 of the pre-trial brief in order to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honour, the Prosecution has studied this matter over the weekend and has come prepared today to propose a solution, if it is satisfactory to the Chamber as well as to the accused. And if I may, with the assistance of the usher, I'd like to pass around a draft paragraph 11 with the insertion of a new sentence, which will bring paragraph 11 of the amended indictment hopefully 100 per cent align with the theory of the case -- in line, I should say, with the theory of the case as described in paragraph 83 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. So if I could ask the usher to pass these around, please, to the Chamber, to the legal officer, and to the Defence counsel and the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It would be nice if I also got one. Thank you. Are you now reading from the original indictment or from the amended -- proposed amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution understands that in the amended indictment the -- it is possible to read the second sentence as implying that Ljube Boskoski had superior responsibility for the acts committed by prison guards, hospital personnel, and civilians, and we understand that this is certainly the issue that the Trial Chamber wishes the Prosecution to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In paragraph 83 of our pre-trial brief, we -- the Prosecution attempts to address this issue, and the Prosecution's proposed solution is to provide a sentence that is almost identical to the second sentence of paragraph 83 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief to -- and add that sentence to paragraph 11 so that the penultimate sentence of paragraph 11 of the amended indictment would now read as follows: "Although Ljube Boskoski was not the superior of prison guards, hospital personnel, and civilians within the meaning of Article 7(3) of the Statute, his criminal responsibility for the acts committed by such persons arises as a result of his failure to punish the regular, reserve, or special police for their acts or omissions which aided and abetted those prison guards, hospital personnel, and other civilians to commit those acts." Your Honour, the Prosecution suggests that with the addition of this language then paragraph 11 will be hopefully crystal clear as to the parameters of the superior responsibility of Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I assume the Defence is not surprised by this formulation because it is already contained in the pre-trial brief. So would you like to comment to this amendment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, would I like to comment. We believe that the issue of amending the indictment was stressed by the Prosecution in its proposal to amend the indictment, which was partially accepted by the Trial Chamber. We believe that the subject of discussion of today's Status Conference could not be a new amendment to the indictment regardless of the fact that in the pre-trial brief submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor there have been indications that such amendment is possible. The Defence of the accused Boskoski is reserving the right to stress all the objections that it has available in terms of Rule 72 from the Rules of Procedure, and we believe that this is an issue that has to be reviewed based by the Trial Chamber. So in the further proceedings of this Status Conference, we have nothing else to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Would you like to add something to what has been said by your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: I do not wish to add anything. I support my colleague totally, although this does not pertain to Johan Tarculovski, this amendment -- this proposed amendment to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there may be some misunderstanding. I'm not quite clear about it. Of course, there are two issues involved. One question, whether this amendment should be made part of an amended indictment or whether it should simply only be dealt with in this conference, Status Conference. And I -- it was my opinion that, I think for the reasons of clarity, because the indictment has to be clear, it's one of the basic documents for the defendants -- for the accused to know what they are charged with, that this amendment should be made part of a newly edited indictment. And so when we discuss it now today, it's only because we are together here I want to clarify this issue. So may I ask the Prosecution what your -- what you had in mind, whether you had planned to amend the indictment anyhow in this -- in this direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the answer to your question, in short, yes. Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution, given the observations made by the Senior Legal Officer which were affirmed by Defence counsel at the Pre-Trial Conference [sic] last Friday, there is arguably a lack of clarity in the indictment. It is then the Prosecution's obligation to do whatever it can to correct that possible lack of clarity in interests of the fair trial right of the accused. So quite frankly, Your Honour, that is how we look at this issue, and unless we are told differently by the Trial Chamber, we would in the near future seek to file a motion proposing that paragraph 11 be amended with the language suggested by the Prosecution today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what we are going to do is that we will further examine the amended -- the proposed amended indictment and compare it with the pre-trial brief in order to find out whether there are any modifications or discrepancies between both and, if so, we would advise both parties, of course in particular the Prosecution but also giving notice to the Defence whether there is need for clarifications and modifications, and if necessary so we may invite both parties to another meeting where these issues will be further discussed. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave I with like to state in relation to what was said by the Prosecutor that the Trial Chamber's order in relation to the form of the indictment stated that the Prosecutor in the pre-trial brief needs to explain in detail in what way it was possible that our client, Mr. Boskoski, was superior to the prison guards and hospital personnel. In this new proposal, as far as I can see, the Prosecution goes beyond this order of the Trial Chamber and claims now, or so it appears, that these acts described in count 11 were actually committed by policemen and not by prison guards or hospital personnel. This was not previously mentioned either in the request to amend the indictment or in the Trial Chamber's order. Based on that, I believe that it would be useful for the Prosecution to file a formal request to amend the indictment so that all of us can be given an opportunity to state our views and positions regarding this. In this case, the indictment is being amended in order to be put in conformity with the pre-trial brief, and it is not done on the basis of the Trial Chamber's order where a clarification was sought in relation to civilians. Thank you for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. If the Prosecution would like to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. What the Prosecution has proposed today was done at the request and I believe with the -- of the Senior Legal Officer who certainly represents the Chamber at a Rule 65 ter Status Conference held three days ago with Defence counsel. That's why we have come forward today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: As I already stated or -- that before, it was indeed the function of the order of - what was it - of November something that we wanted the Prosecution to clarify this position, and as far as I can see, the clarification which has been put forward today is in conformity with what had been in the pre-trial brief and what's now necessary is to make this modification or amendment, to introduce it as part of the indictment, and this should be done in the same way as any amendments to the indictment are normally made according to the Rules. But as I already indicated, we will go over the amended indictment once more in comparing it with the pre-trial brief in order to find out whether there are any other -- whether there is any other need for clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of the accused Boskoski entirely understands your comments and understands them -- the comments made by the senior legal officer at the 65 ter Conference which was held on Friday. However, the Defence can -- further remains that in the given case we cannot speak about an explanation, clarification, as it was referred by my learned friend to this document. According to our opinion, this is a new indictment, actually amendments to the indictment, and we believe that this should not be allowed at this stage of the proceedings where we have a confirmed amended indictment. We believe that the Prosecution can clarify the indictment per se. However, the Prosecution cannot, from sources like pre-trial brief, to come up with a new crimes that will be alleged to the accused such as the second sentence which we have received today to the paragraph 11 of the amended indictment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I understand your position. We will examine it and then we will come down with the necessary orders and clarifications. Thank you very much. Now, the Defence pre-trial brief, as you are all aware, could be postponed because the original Scheduling Order had to be changed, and for that reason I will now come to outstanding motions. There was a motion by the Defence with regard to production of evidence from a state filed on the 20 October 2005 by the accused Tarculovski. As you have been made aware, there was a response by the Prosecution stating that it does not oppose the position, the motion, and then I had sent a letter to the government of the Former Yugoslavian Republic of Macedonia on 23rd of November. We got a response from them and I was just informed before we started this session that the translation of this letter -- of this material is supposed to be finished by December 21st. And once it is completed, this translation, the Trial Chamber will examine the translated letter and take further measures in accordance with Rule 54 and 54 bis. So to sum up this point, the Trial Chamber will take necessary steps, if required, after the translation of the letter and after receipt of the letter, and then we'll come forward again. The next outstanding motion regards a motion by the Prosecution with regard to protective measures, non-disclosure to the public. Neither accused filed a response to it. I was informed that this issue was discussed in the 65 ter meeting to some length, and I just would like to state what the position of the Chamber is. I always the Pre-Trial Judge would like to reaffirm that the protective measures relevant to non-disclosure to the public order in the Prosecution's decision on the motion for protection of victims and witnesses issued on 20 June 2005 cover any of the material and the identity of any witness or group of witnesses provided by the Prosecution to the Defence. This decision also covers the material provided to the Defence under Rule 65 ter of the Rules. Consequently, the Prosecution's motion for protective measures filed with the pre-trial brief on 7 November 2005 is moot. As Pre-Trial Judge, I also remind the parties that the decision on -- of June 20, 2005, covers the statements of potential witnesses who are not on the witness list any more as a result of the Prosecution's decisions not to call or who the Prosecution may decide not to call at a later stage. So much to this pending motion. Another pending motion relating -- other pending motions relate to disclosure. There are three pending motions relevant to disclosure. In chronological order the first one is a motion with respect to Rule 68 material filed by Mr. Boskoski, a motion with respect to Rule 66(A)(ii) and implicitly Rule 66(A)(i) and 65 ter(E)(iii) material also filed by Mr. Boskoski, and then a motion with respect to Rule 66 (A)(ii) material filed by Mr. Tarculovski. All this has been discussed in the 65 ter Conference. As Pre-Trial Judge, I confirm that the Chamber will soon issue a Scheduling Order setting various deadlines for the completion of various disclosure obligations. Now, with regard to these pending motions, is there any submission at this point of our conference? If this is not the case, we can continue with the status of various disclosure issues. The first point refers to Rule 66(A)(i) material. This is material supporting to the indictment. This also has been discussed in the pre-trial -- 65 ter Conference. We have been informed that the Defence had some difficulties to bring DVDs and CDs to the accused or had to submit such material for inspection at the United Nations Detention Unit. Understand the Defence counsel's concerns that it might infringe the confidentiality stemming from the counsel/client privilege. As you may remember, the senior legal officer stated this needed to be resolved through further discussion, and I would like to tell you that the senior legal officer has the full support of the Trial Chamber to find a solution, an arrangement with the Registry, in particular with the Detention Unit, which may be -- satisfy your concerns. Now, in with regard to this material, I would -- as the Pre-Trial Judge I would like -- I would set a deadline for the completion of the translation of additional supporting material as Rule 66(A)(i) provides for very strict deadlines in this regard. I intend to set a deadline for completion by the end of January 2006, and I think that's quite serious. The accused should be made -- should be put in a position to collect this material in an understandable way as soon as possible. There is a submission from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Simply a question for clarification, Your Honour. There is a portion of supporting material that supported the recent amendments to the indictment that is now being translated by the CLSS, the Registry's Translation Unit. The CLSS, I believe, has made inquiries as to whether the entire body of that supporting material, which is hundreds and hundreds of pages, must be translated into the language of the accused or whether it is only the relevant portions of that original material that were designated by the Prosecution as supporting its theory that the armed conflict in Macedonia in 2001 continued through September of that year. The difference in terms of labour and time, of course, required by CLSS to do this work will be substantial depending on the direction of the Trial Chamber. I would simply request respectfully that the Trial Chamber clarify that point if it could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: We will do so. I think at this point now it would be -- I would like to avoid a quick decision. I would like to go into this issue and to inform the Prosecution and the parties, of course, as soon as possible on this point. Now we come to the next issue, material with regard to Rule 66(A)(ii), so-called witness statements' material. We have been informed that the Prosecution will call I think about 125 witnesses in total in a chart which had been presented in the 65 ter meeting. I think also to the Defence, which I think is very helpful, to get an idea what's going on. We have already been informed that witness statements of 104 witnesses, that runs up to 80 per cent of the total statements, are already disclosed both in English and Macedonian. Indeed you are working very hard on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon the introduction. We have an updated chart if Your Honour would so like to receive since there has been additional disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Would you also have copies for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. If Mr. Usher could provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. There have been five Macedonian translations outstanding, and these seem to be translated in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So I hope that the Defence can agree with me that the Prosecution is trying to do its best. Okay. Now, as the Pre-Trial Judge, I would like to include in the Scheduling Order a deadline for the completion of this -- this list. Wait a minute. I will also issue a Scheduling Order setting a deadline for the completion of this 66(A)(ii) disclosure, and this order will require a continuation of disclosure of new statements in English and Macedonian on an ongoing basis, and completion of this process by the end of March. And please believe me, this deadline is not just taken arbitrarily but, since case should be ready for trial as soon as possible, we think there should be some -- some effort put into completing this exercise. Mr. Saxon. You have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution takes note of the date mentioned by the -- by Your Honour, and we will work a hundred per cent of our efforts to meet that deadline. I would just like to note one potential caveat and that is simply that, with regard to disclosure of all statements in the language of the accused, in this case Macedonian, oftentimes the CLSS unit is under tremendous pressure, not only of course from this case but from the demands of many other cases, and it may at least certainly be within the realm of possibility that some translations may not be available until beyond the 31st of March, but certainly the Prosecution will do everything in its power to ensure that all statements in English that all counsel can understand and read will be provided to the accused prior to the end of March, and any translations of those statements in Macedonian as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course as nobody -- the Prosecution as well cannot be asked to do the impossible, but you should be -- really take all efforts, and I understand you said you would do it, to finalise this exercise by the end of March. Is there anything from the Defence side to this point now? It doesn't look like it. Now we come to Rule 65 ter(E)(iii) which concerns exhibits and objections to the authenticity made by the Defence against certain exhibits. Out of -- as I have been informed from the 65 ter meeting, out of 309 exhibits on the exhibit list, 25 exhibits are yet to be translated in Macedonian and 284 exhibits are disclosed both in English and Macedonian. And here again we have a very helpful chart from the Prosecution, exhibits on Rule 65 ter list, where you can also see the numbers I just gave to you. As Pre-Trial Judge, I will include in the Scheduling Order all the deadline of the completion of the exhibit list. This deadline will be identical as for the completion 66(A)(ii) list. So the Prosecution is required to update its exhibit list by the end of March 2006. And I would like to add the Prosecution is required to include in that exhibit list all the exhibits that may form part of any expert reports the Prosecution intends to have produced. Now I would come to Rule 68 material, so-called exculpatory material which is of particular importance, of course, for the Defence, meaning that if the Prosecution comes over material which may mitigate or even give indications for innocence of the accused, this should be disclosed to the Defence. This question again has been has dealt with in detail in the 65 ter Conference. I was informed that the Defence has certain problems in getting along with EDS, to use all the possibilities which may be available by using EDS, but that the Prosecution is willing to cooperate with the Defence in terms of the search training on EDS. So what I would like to confirm is the following: First, that I was informed about the progress being made in this respect, also on the completion of the present 68 searches undertaken by the Prosecution, I will include a deadline for completion in the Scheduling Order which I had mentioned before. Now, having gone through the disclosure issues, are there any other issues that the parties what like to include under all 65 ter, 66, or 68. Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, just a point of clarification when you refer to the completion of the Prosecution's disclosure work pursuant to Rule 68. The Prosecution takes its obligation under this Rule very seriously and in our response to the accused Boskoski's motion regarding Rule 68, we've laid out I think fairly clearly the efforts we're making in this regard. However, of course, Your Honour used the word "completion," and, of course, as you know, the language of the Rule refers to the ongoing obligation, and we are working well, I think, with the -- with Defence counsel. Just today we had another meeting with the counsel for the accused Boskoski, and we received a letter from the accused Boskoski that dealt with sort of an additional request for material that might result in indeed more, possibly more, exculpatory material. So I'm just raising this as a point of clarification to understand what will be -- when the Chamber using the word "completion," what is the scope of that term within the Chamber's understanding? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Mr. Saxon, that you mentioned this issue. I think the term "completion" in this context may not be the best one. It maybe understood, particularly because it is really an ongoing process, and what is meant it what you should of course -- there is a great bulk of material which has to be disclosed very soon, but as soon as you are -- as soon as you become aware of material you should digs close it as your earliest convenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and the Prosecution I tends to do that. With respect to the 145 searches that the Prosecution is currently undertaking for potentially exculpatory material, the Prosecution believes that those searches will be completed by the end of February. Some of them have been completed already, as you know, and any additional then material identified as relevant or exculpatory from those searches will be disclosed to the accused by the end of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: That may be the issue that the -- perhaps the Defence may not be completely aware of this. Sometimes it can really happen -- just a minute. It can happen after the Prosecution have thought they have disclosed everything, then they find something else, and then -- of course, the Prosecution may say there was a violation of 68, but if the Prosecution comes up with newly found material which it wasn't able to get hold of earlier, you could not so easily consider it a violation of Rule 68. Now, you wanted to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Boskoski hereby confirms that from mid-November the Prosecution last been in compliance with their obligation under this rule. They have started disclosing to us material uncovered by them through their searches. We fully understand this is a continuous obligation on the part of the Prosecution and that they will comply with it the throughout the proceedings. Another issue you brought up are the problems that we encountered with the EDS system. We discussed this issue during our 65 ter Conference, and we wish to repeat it in front you will now, Your Honour, that the searches we have conducted on the EDS system so far and all our attempts at finding exculpatory material have not yielded any results so far, for the simple reason this is the first case of the events dealing with regards in Macedonia and there is no material about it available on the EDS. We hope that the Prosecution will put a large amount of material on the EDS system so that we can conduct searches ourselves. In relation to this issue, we have talked to the Prosecution, as my learned friend has already stated, and we have discussed some other issues, namely our request pursuant to Rule 68. The Prosecution confirmed to us that they have four Albanian cases and that they will use that criteria and another criteria to conduct searches. They also confirmed to us that they have material related to international organisations which were present in Macedonia during the relevant period of time. However, the OTP told us that they would not disclose the entire material of that nature but only those portions which either, in their view, fall under Rule 68 or, two, which do not have any limitations under Rule 68(i) which do not have any limitations under Rule 70. In view of that, Your Honour, we wish to inform you that we will file a motion requesting disclosure of that material under Rule 66(B), because it's undisputable that the Prosecution has this material, and the Defence will state the reasons it believes that this material is of great importance for the preparation of our Defence. Another issue: Nearly relating to Ljube and the time frame referred in the indictment are not the only issues that we will require disclosure of material, because we want material pertaining to the entire situation in Macedonia, all of the events taking place there which are covered by the entire context of the indictment, from January to September, as is stated in the new amended indictment. The Defence is interested in all of that material, and we have told the Prosecution about that and told them that we would soon be filing a motion under Rule 66(B). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You would like to respond to it directly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly. As of the close of business Friday, 9 December, three days ago, I'm told that the entire evidentiary collection of the Office of the Prosecutor related to events in Macedonia, about the exception of Rule 70 material and sensitive witness statements, will be available on the EDS. So it should now be available and hopefully the searches of Defence counsel will be much more productive starting today. Related to the point that Ms. Residovic raised that they will soon be filing a motion under Rule 66(B) because it is undisputable that the Prosecution -- that was Ms. Residovic's word, or what I heard in translation, the Prosecution will certainly honour any valid request, request with a legitimate legal purpose and will seek to find any such material it has in its collections pursuant to such a valid request of the Defence. We would ask simply that such requests be as specific as possible to enable the Prosecution to search for these materials and disclose them as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Without saying a final word on this, with regard to the problems with EDS, I would like to make clear two points with regard to the -- how to make -- do it. You may be aware that I'm of a generation where we have not yet been so firm in doing things like this. I cannot give you any assistance. I have to completely rely on other people. And I am glad if I understand at all what's going about. But I am quite sure that the assistance which is offered to you from the Prosecution will help you in this record. The more legal problem, of course, is the issue which has been addressed from your side, Mr. Saxon. I think you are clear about the position of this Chamber that it is not enough just to say now you have all the -- to say to the Defence, "Now you have everything on EDS and look how you get around with it." There is a -- 68(ii) contains an obligation on the Prosecution side to identify material which may be exculpatory. Now, I -- what I think and I had the impression that you also wanted to say it this way: The Defence may submit their motion, and you should be indeed as clear as possible, as specific as possible, to make it easier for the Prosecution what you are asking for and then we have to find a way which is satisfying to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution fully understands the position of the Trial Chamber on this issue, and that is why, for example, if you look at the pie chart number 3 that was provided to the Chamber last Friday, you will see in graphic detail the fact that the Prosecution is not solely relying on the fact that there is an electronic disclosure system available for the use of the accused. On the contrary. We have initiated searches of over 145 separate terms across the OTP's evidentiary collections. We have completed some of those searches and the reviews of some of that material, and we have provided material that was specifically identified in those searches, to 35 of those such searches already to the accused. It is the Prosecution, then, in this case is simply taking the position that certainly the availability of the EDS, electronic disclosure system, makes it possible for the Defence -- for Defence counsel to locate material on their own because there is always the possibility quite frankly, particularly with differences in language, that the Prosecution to miss something. And this is a way of making as much material possible available and accessible to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So just to make it clear and I have the impression that we agree on this point, it was not your position to say since you have EDS it is your job and we are relieved of all obligations. You say the Defence may on their own also try to find out as much as possible what may be important for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is exactly the position of the Prosecution, and quite frankly, Your Honour, in the interests of protecting the fair trial rights of the accused, we would encourage the Defence to make use of the electronic disclosure system, because, quite frankly again, they may find this material more quickly than the Prosecution do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I think you got this point. I mean, you also have to realise from the Defence that, assuming that the Prosecution is always acting in good faith, even if they are acting in good faith there may be material that to them, to their judgement, may not appear mitigating but it may appear mitigating from your position, I think, for this reason. I think it should be your own interest also to get into this material and if you identify something to get hold of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have fully understood the position of the Prosecution and the position of Your Honour, and in this context I would like to indicate that so far the Defence and the Prosecution in their regular communication which we have had with several briefs and motions we have requested. A specific material which is of exculpatory character according to the Rule 68. In this respect, in our regular meetings, as today and in future, we have discussed which materials -- material could be a material according to 68 Rule, and in future we are aware of our obligation to communicate with the Prosecution, and if the Defence has any knowledge of a material could be in the Prosecution files and which could have an exculpatory nature, we would like to reserve right, and it will be our duty to request such materials from the Prosecution, and we believe that they would be responsive and that they will fulfil their obligation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So to come to an end with this point, we -- you are awaiting or expecting some motion from your side in this area. Thank you. Now, the next point I would like to address is the problems of Rule 92 bis statements. This Rule deals with the proof of facts other than oral -- by oral evidence, or you could say proof by way of introducing by way of written statements. So far 53 witness statements will be presented under Rule 92 bis. The Prosecution stated in the Pre-Trial Conference that it was preparing a Rule 92 bis motion providing more than 40 witness statements. Also, it wanted to wait for such a filing until a Bench would have been appointed that would hear the case. But as has been indicated by the senior legal officer, the Bench thinks you should not wait until the Trial Bench is finally appointed. And I concur that the Prosecution is to file more than one motion pursuant to Rule 92 bis in order to allow the Defence and the Chamber to properly prepare for a response and decision to such motions. Before I continue, would you like to make a submission in this respect or -- because you seem to -- wanted to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So in the Scheduling Order, I will indicate that a first 92 bis motion needs to be submitted in the course of January, and the last motion again before the end of March 2006 upon completion of Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure. That would be the position of the Chamber. Now, are there any other matters either party wish to raise on this subject apart from what has already been discussed at the Rule 65 ter Conference? If this is not the case, I would come to Rule 94 bis statements which concerns testimony of expert witnesses. If I include the updating by the Prosecution, there will be four expert witness statements presented under Rule 94 bis. Also, the filing of expert reports will be included in the Scheduling Order. I intend to order that to have all expert reports submitted by the end of March of 2006 in English subject to translation into Macedonian as soon as possible thereafter. Is there any reaction from the parties in -- with regard to this issue of testimony of expert witnesses? This doesn't seem to be the case. So I come to the question of length of trial and planning of trial. As you have become aware, the original plans of starting this trial even by the end of this year has been -- this plan has been superseded by a different scheduling of the Tribunal by taking the Martic case and giving the Martic case precedence over the Boskoski and Tarculovski case. And as you remember, the main reason has been that the Martic case has been much longer dealt with in this court and that the defendant -- the accused is detained for a much longer time than the present accused, and for this reason the Martic case had to take precedence. But nevertheless, the Trial Chamber and the Tribunal is very much interested to get this case ready as soon as possible, probably in late spring, May or June, and this means that having this state in mind the pre-trial briefs also have to be presented accordingly, and this will also be dealt with in the Scheduling Order. Now, if I may sum up what we have discussed and what we have agreed about and if not finalised how we could proceed, I would like to give you the following points: First, I will soon issue a Scheduling Order setting a number of deadlines for the Prosecution to further complete their preparations for trial. Once these deadlines have been met, it will be time to set a deadline for the preparation of a pre-trial brief by the Defence. Secondly, the Prosecution will be ordered to complete their further preparations for the trial in the course of March and some parts of it even before that. I think I don't have to go into details. Third, the parties will be ordered to negotiate proposed agreed facts during the course of April and May. And fourth, by the end of May or early June, the pre-trial brief of the Defence will be due. And I think that gives you enough time really to have a thorough and solid pre-trial brief which takes care of all the concerns your clients may have. Now, are there any other comments either party wish to make on the scheduling for the pre-trial procedures and the planning of the trial apart from what has already been discussed at the Rule 65 ter Conference? There is no request for doing so. And so finally do any of the parties wish to raise any other matters? This is not the case. And now I would like personally to address the accused. Mr. Boskoski and Mr. Tarculovski, would you like to raise any matter relating to your state of health or your condition of detention? And before you start to say something, you should be advised once more this is not the place to raise any issues with regard to the indictment and so on. There are two questions which may be dealt with now, the state of your health and if you have any complaints with regard to the condition of the detention. Mr. Boskoski, would you like to take the floor. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to say that the conditions in the new building where we have been transferred now since several days ago are quite good, that it is incomparably better than in the building where we used to be. Our health status -- at least my health status is fine. I think that psychologically and physically I'm sustaining and I expect that the trial will start as soon as possible so that I am able physically and psychologically fit to defend my innocence and the innocence of my home country Macedonia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Boskoski. Mr. Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: His microphone is not on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: He has it on now. Your microphone. Does it work now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No. We don't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could you raise it as much as possible or -- perhaps you start and if you cannot be heard --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, that is fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: That is fine. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my health situation is also fine. I don't have any problems. But the comments -- the problems we feel we have in the detention, we have the same from since we arrived here. For nine months we have submitted at least ten motions to have our Macedonian television broadcasted in the prison, because all the other detainees have the opportunity to follow their own TVs apart from us. We feel discriminated in comparison to others. And we have some small problems regarding our requests, motions -- requests we don't have in our own language, requests for visits, for interviews or -- we -- they're not translated into our native language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was not aware of this problem. As you know, I personally cannot do very much about this language or translation or TV problems. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was a representative from the court some two or three months ago. We personally discussed it with him and we emphasised this problem that we were facing, and we were told that as soon as possible, possibly within a month, we would be accommodated with the TV, but this has -- for nine months already we are waiting. We have submitted more than ten requests maybe, or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Although I have do not have jurisdiction with this question, I will personally address the registrar and ask what personally can be done about it. But I have to inform you of your formal rights. If you have any complaints with regard to detention, pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules -- 85 of the Rules of Detention, you have a complaint procedure and you may use this in order to get settled any concerns you may have. Thank you very much. Now, there seems to be no further issue to be dealt with now. Since we are rather close to the end of this year, I would like to wish everybody good season's greetings. Of course we are aware that the conditions are different for those of you that are in the position of an accused than the other ones, but nevertheless I also hope that you can celebrate these days with some confidence in the New Year. So best wishes to all of you, and with this I would like to adjourn our meeting, our conference. Thank you very much.
